title: Continuatio Fragmentorum ex Adversariis mathematicis depromptorum

deep.reconstruction:
Context (pp. 500–502). On the previous page Euler expands ∫dφ(1+k cos2φ)^{-1/2} and ∫dφ cos2φ (1+k cos2φ)^{-1/2} over 0..π/2. He obtains CN−AM = ½aπ√(k/2)·Σ(−1)^j c_j k^j with c_j = (1/2)_j /(2^j ⌊j/2⌋! ⌈j/2⌉!). Setting k=1 gives 2√2/π = 1 − 1/4 + 1·3/(4·4) − 1·3·5/(4·4·8) + … . In modern form, s − t = (2/π)∫_0^{π/2}(1+cos2φ)(1+k cos2φ)^{-1/2}dφ, which at k=1 equals (2/π)∫√2 cosφ dφ = 2√2/π.

He then splits the series into even and odd parts. With k = z², s = Σ a_n z^{4n} = ₂F₁(1/4,3/4;1;z⁴) and t = Σ b_n z^{4n+2} = (z²/4)·₂F₁(3/4,5/4;2;z⁴). The two differential relations from p.500 give s = (1−z⁴)t'/z + (2−z⁴)t/z².

On this page:
(1) Eliminating s gives the second-order linear ODE z²(1−z⁴)t'' + z(1−5z⁴)t' − (4+3z⁴)t = 0. In the variable x = z⁴ this is a hypergeometric equation.
(2) The substitution t = exp∫ν dz yields the Riccati equation z²(1−z⁴)(ν'+ν²) + z(1−5z⁴)ν − (4+3z⁴) = 0.
(3) Putting ν = q/(z(1−z⁴)) simplifies this to dq + q²dz/(z(1−z⁴)) − (4+3z⁴)dz/z = 0. Here q = z(1−z⁴)t'/t, so s = t(q+2−z⁴)/z². The thread is not pursued.
(4) Lemma, the Beta-function recurrence: ∫_0^1 z^{m+n−1}(1−z^n)^{k−1}dz = m/(m+kn) ∫_0^1 z^{m−1}(1−z^n)^{k−1}dz.
(5) 'Alia methodus': expand (1−k²z⁴)^{-1/4} binomially and choose a weight dp so that the moments ∫z^{4n}dp/∫dp = (3/4)_n/n!. The lemma with n=4, k=1/4 gives dp = z²dz/(1−z⁴)^{3/4}. Hence s = ∫z²dz(1−z⁴)^{-3/4}(1−k²z⁴)^{-1/4} : ∫z²dz(1−z⁴)^{-3/4}. With u = z⁴ this is exactly Euler's integral representation of ₂F₁(1/4,3/4;1;k²).
(6) For t he uses ((1−k²z⁴)^{-1/4}−1)/(kz²) with dp = dz/(1−z⁴)^{3/4}. On the next page he concludes t = ∫dz((1−k²z⁴)^{-1/4}−1)/(kz²(1−z⁴)^{3/4}) : ∫dz/(1−z⁴)^{3/4}. He then remarks that this does not show how the series can be expressed more conveniently.

The purpose throughout is to find closed or integral forms for the series arising in the geometric (curve-length) problem of p.500. In modern terms s = (2/π)∫_0^{π/2}(1+k cos2φ)^{-1/2}dφ = (2/π)(1+k)^{-1/2}K(√(2k/(1+k))), a complete elliptic integral (quadratic transformation of ₂F₁).
errors: The normalization for t (completed on p.502) is wrong. The required moment ratios are ∫z^{4n−2}dp / D = (3/4)_{n−1}/(n−1)!, which forces D = ∫_0^1 z²dz/(1−z⁴)^{3/4} = π√2/4 ≈ 1.1107. Euler instead divides by ∫_0^1 dz/(1−z⁴)^{3/4} = Γ(1/4)²/(4√π) ≈ 1.854. His formula therefore gives t multiplied by ≈0.599: the leading term comes out ≈0.6·k/4 instead of k/4. The lemma cannot link z² with z⁰ here, since that would need m = −1, so the step 'Hinc dp = dz/(1−z⁴)^{3/4}' fixes dp correctly but the denominator must be ∫z²dp.

Not an error, but worth noting: s and t each diverge logarithmically at k=1, since c−a−b = 0 for ₂F₁(1/4,3/4;1;·). Only s−t converges there, so the integral representations cannot be evaluated separately at k=1 to recover 2√2/π.

Checked and correct: the ODE (the recurrence (4n+4)(4n+8)b_{n+1} = (4n+3)(4n+5)b_n reproduces b_1 = 15/128 and b_2 = 945/12288), the expression of s through t, the Riccati reduction, the substitution ν = q/(z(1−z⁴)), the lemma (Beta ratio), and the integral formula for s.

ideas.what: Second-order linear ODE satisfied by the odd part of the series, reducible to the hypergeometric equation in x = z⁴
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Institutiones calculi integralis II, 1769; E710); Gauss 1812
ideas.where_published: Institutiones calculi integralis vol. II (E366); 'Specimen transformationis singularis serierum' (E710)

ideas.what: Reduction of a second-order linear ODE to a Riccati equation via t = exp∫ν
ideas.where_published: Institutiones calculi integralis II and many earlier papers
E321 and related papers on ∫x^{p−1}(1−x^n)^{q/n−1}; Inst. calc. int. I

ideas.what: Choosing a weight dp so its moments reproduce the extra Pochhammer factor, giving s as a ratio of Euler-type integrals
ideas.modern_name: Euler integral representation of ₂F₁(1/4,3/4;1;k²) (moment / Hausdorff-type method)
ideas.where_published: Inst. calc. int. II (E366), ch. on series from integrals; E710

ideas.what: The series 1 − 1/4 + 1·3/(4·4) − … = 2√2/π (from p.500), split into even and odd parts
ideas.modern_name: special value of a combination of contiguous ₂F₁ at the singular point

missed.claim: Euler leaves the series s and t without closed form ('neutiquam patet') and drops the Riccati thread. In modern terms s = ₂F₁(1/4,3/4;1;k²) = (1+k)^{-1/2}·₂F₁(1/2,1/2;1;2k/(1+k)), i.e. a complete elliptic integral via a quadratic transformation, so the 'commodius' expression he sought exists. This is a historical observation, not new mathematics.
missed.quote: Hinc autem neutiquam patet quomodo haec series commodius exprimi possit.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only as a historical illustration: Euler had the integral representation and ODE in hand but not the quadratic transformation (later Gauss/Kummer). It has no research value today.

deep.surprise_reason: Competent, mostly routine manipulations: hypergeometric ODE, Riccati reduction, Beta recurrence, and Euler integral representation. All are techniques Euler published elsewhere. The interesting bits are an early-looking use of a moment-matching weight to represent ₂F₁ and an unnoticed normalization slip for t. Neither amounts to a missed result.
transcription_corrections: None substantive; the transcription matches the image. Note that the wrong denominator ∫dz/(1−z⁴)^{3/4} for t on p.502 is in the printed text, not a transcription error.
